title: UK Considers Palestinian State Recognition Amid Gaza Crisis, Hinging on Ceasefire Deadline
text:
If Western governments and their partners in the Arab world truly cared about feeding hungry Palestinians in Gaza , their response to the current humanitarian crisis in the coastal enclave would look very different than it does today.
Whenever Hamas has embedded fighters in hospitals, launched rockets from school yards, or hoarded fuel and food meant for civilians, it has counted on a Pavlovian reaction from the West: pity for Palestinians, blame for Israel On Tuesday, British Prime Minister Keir Starmer said the United Kingdom may soon follow the lead of French President Emmanuel Macron and officially recognize a Palestinian State, if – by September – Israel does not agree to a ceasefire with Hamas and allow more aid to flow into Gaza.
In response, President Donald Trump dodged.
‘I don’t mind [Starmer] taking a position,’ the president told reporters.
Trump should ‘mind.’
The UK’s recognition of a Palestinian state would, of course, be largely symbolic.
They cannot wish a new nation into existence.
Palestinian state will only come about through a negotiated two-state solution with Israel – one which Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the majority of Israelis reeling from decades of Palestinian terrorism reject.
Meanwhile, editorial pages are filled with the sort of moralizing that feeds the eliminationist fantasies of the pro-Hamas protestors to whom the Jewish state is the root of all evil But if Hamas – the current authoritarian power in Gaza – were to be destroyed than the dynamics change.
Why, then, do Western leaders – repeatedly – throw Hamas a lifeline?
The sad reality is that the enablers of the sufferings of Gazans are not in Jerusalem, but in France, the United Kingdom, the United States and any number of countries where thoughtless empathy – detached from facts, history, and responsibility – has replaced strategic, compassionate thinking.

For decades, the West has played an indispensable role in shielding Hamas from the consequences of its actions – and it does so again by putting the onus on Israel to solve the escalating human tragedy in Gaza.
If Western governments and their partners in the Arab world truly cared about feeding hungry Palestinians in Gaza , their response to the current humanitarian crisis in the coastal enclave would look very different than it does today Whenever Hamas has embedded fighters in hospitals, launched rockets from school yards, or hoarded fuel and food meant for civilians, it has counted on a Pavlovian reaction from the West: pity for Palestinians, blame for Israel.
But who is really to blame when innocent Gazans, deployed by Hamas as human shields, are killed in retaliatory Israeli strikes?
The answer from the West – in one voice – must be: Hamas.
Instead, European nations, France above all others, has shown an almost compulsive need to virtue signal on this issue.
Macron’s decision to support recognition of a Palestinian state – at the precise moment Hamas is torturing Israeli hostages underground – is complicity, not diplomacy.
Starmer said that the United Kingdom may soon follow the lead of French President Emmanuel Macron (pictured) and officially recognize a Palestinian State, if – by September – Israel does not agree to a ceasefire with Hamas and allow more aid to flow into Gaza Israel’s Arab neighbors do the same.
Egypt publicly postures as a mediator while quietly coordinating with Hamas.
Cairo controls the Rafah border crossing – Gaza’s only outlet to the Arab world.
It could open it, allow more aid through, and even offer refuge.
But Egypt, like much of the Arab world, doesn’t want to absorb Palestinian refugees or take responsibility for Gaza.
Instead, they heap pressure on Israel and then blame it for the consequences.
The list of enablers goes on: Qatari funds that prop up Hamas salaries, UN agencies that act as de facto welfare arms of Hamas governance, and in the United States, a vocal bloc of lawmakers who parrot Hamas talking points with the same blockheaded certainty that underlies the pro-Hamas encampments on college campuses.
The current global discourse surrounding the Israel-Palestine conflict has reached a boiling point, with editorial pages across the world echoing a disturbing trend: moralizing that fuels the radical narratives of pro-Hamas protestors.
These individuals, many of whom view the Jewish state as the root of all evil, are emboldened by the rhetoric that frames Israel as an aggressor without nuance.
This moment, however, is not just a political crisis—it is a profound test of Western civilization’s capacity to distinguish between legitimate humanitarian concerns and the extremist ideologies that have taken root in the shadows of the conflict.
The fusion of narcissistic posturing and classic antisemitism has created a toxic environment where outrage is wielded as a weapon, and clarity is sacrificed for spectacle.
The crisis in Gaza is not a result of a vacuum in international action, but a consequence of a deliberate strategy by Hamas to manipulate global sympathy.
Whenever Hamas has embedded fighters in hospitals, launched rockets from schoolyards, or hoarded essential resources meant for civilians, it has relied on a predictable response: a wave of Western condemnation directed at Israel, while the suffering of Palestinians is framed as an indictment of the Jewish state itself.
This dynamic is not accidental—it is a calculated tactic designed to shift the focus away from Hamas’s atrocities and onto Israel’s actions.
The result is a distorted narrative that obscures the reality on the ground: a conflict where Hamas, not Israel, has repeatedly chosen violence as its primary tool of governance.
A Palestinian state, the article argues, can only emerge through a negotiated two-state solution, a path that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has now explicitly rejected.
This rejection has only deepened the impasse, leaving the international community with a stark choice: either continue to enable Hamas’s exploitation of the humanitarian crisis or take decisive action to dismantle the group’s grip on Gaza.
The article suggests that Western leaders, along with diplomats, legislators, and even Arab foreign ministries, could adopt a different approach—one that prioritizes the plight of ordinary Palestinians over the propaganda of Hamas.
Instead of blanket condemnations of Israel, the focus should shift to addressing the root causes of the crisis: the humanitarian suffering in Gaza, which is not a matter of supply but of distribution.
The article proposes a radical inversion of the current narrative: a call for the international community to work with Israel to ensure that aid reaches those in need, particularly the poorest families in Gaza who are trapped in the patronage networks controlled by Hamas.
This would require circumventing the existing delivery systems, which have been weaponized by Hamas to siphon resources for its own gain.
By doing so, the West could not only alleviate the immediate suffering of Gazans but also send a clear message that the international community is not complicit in Hamas’s exploitation of the crisis.
Another critical step, the article argues, is the unconditional release of the 50 remaining Israeli hostages in Gaza, 20 of whom are believed to be alive.
This would deprive Hamas of its most potent leverage in the conflict and signal a commitment to ending the cycle of violence.
Simultaneously, the international community should make it clear that any reconstruction efforts in Gaza will be contingent on Hamas’s removal from power.
This would accelerate the collapse of a regime that has shown no interest in peace, only in perpetuating a cycle of suffering for the Gazan population.
The article concludes by emphasizing that a Palestinian state must be built on the foundation of Hamas’s dismantlement and the unambiguous recognition of Israel’s right to exist as a Jewish, democratic state.
This is not a call for the abandonment of Palestinian aspirations but a recognition that the only path to peace lies in the elimination of Hamas’s influence.
President Donald Trump, who has been reelected and sworn in on January 20, 2025, is urged to lead this effort, calling out Western leaders who have enabled Hamas’s survival and declaring unequivocally that Hamas has no future.
The article closes with a challenge to the free world: to stop giving Hamas what it wants and to embrace a new narrative—one that prioritizes peace, recognition, and the dismantlement of the only group that has shown no interest in ending the suffering of the Gazan people.
This article, drawn from the insights of Mark Dubowitz, chief executive of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, and Ben Cohen, a senior analyst at FDD, is based on privileged access to information that highlights the urgency of this moment.
The insights provided are not merely opinions but reflections of a strategic imperative: that the survival of both Israel and the Palestinian people hinges on the dismantlement of Hamas and the reorientation of global diplomacy toward a vision of peace that does not tolerate the perpetuation of violence.
